cards.title: Concept Matrix: Persona × Angle × Offer × Ad Type
cards.summary: Build ad concepts as persona/angle/offer/ad-type combinations so each ad set tests a readable, nicheable concept rather than a random batch of creative.
cards.use_when: Structuring acquisition campaigns and ad sets for a store, deciding how to brief creative, or diagnosing why you can't tell which audience message is winning.
steps: Define a matrix with four columns: persona (e.g. coffee drinkers, brides, smokers for a teeth-whitening product), angle (the specific problem/benefit framing, e.g. 'whitening without sensitivity issues' vs 'get ready for your wedding in 14 days'), offer (product only, curated bundle, subscription), and ad type (UGC, testimonial, founder talking head, before/after).
Map each combination to its own ad set so the ad set itself encodes the concept, not just a product. Example: coffee drinkers + whitening without sensitivity + product only + UGC.

Because ad type is flexible and near-infinite within a fixed persona/angle/offer, rotate many creative variations inside the same concept ad set to test execution without changing the concept being measured.
Keep concept as the ad-set-level unit so you can KPI performance by concept rather than only at campaign level, which is what produces directional creative feedback.

Once a concept wins, double down: increase creative volume on that concept, build a matching custom landing page with continuity (same testimonial, same before/after, same language), and align the offer to it (e.g. spin the bundle out as a named '14-day wedding bundle').

Feed winning concepts upstream into landing pages, retention flows and product portfolio; e.g. a strong brides concept can justify a post-wedding win-back flow and cross-sell into another product line.
Use concept-level allocation data (roughly what share of new customers come from each persona/angle) to inform broader business and product strategy.
caveats: Broad, un-niched targeting yields no accurate persona insight and that error propagates into landing pages, retention and portfolio decisions.
The teeth-whitening example is illustrative, not evidence of results.
Custom landing pages and bundles require enough volume to justify the build before you commit.

cards.title: Ad Volume Targets and Ad-to-Ad-Set Ratio at Scale
cards.summary: High-spend stores should launch roughly 100–300 new ads per month, which is manageable inside a small number of campaigns and ad sets.
cards.use_when: Planning monthly creative production and deciding how many campaigns and ad sets your account needs to absorb that output.
steps: At scale, target roughly 100–300 new ads launched per month if growth is the goal; the source notes this volume is not required if you don't want to grow.

Structure to absorb that volume: e.g. two campaigns each holding 10 ad sets = 20 ad sets, which at 100 ads per month is around 5 ads per ad set and at 300 ads per month is around 15 per ad set — both are workable ratios.
You can run fewer campaigns and ad sets than this example and still handle the volume; the constraint is ad-to-ad-set ratio, which stays manageable.
Keep the concept taxonomy (persona/angle/offer/ad type) as the naming and grouping logic so volume stays categorised instead of becoming a random batch dump.

Pair volume with quality standard and strategy; the source describes accounts launching 2,000+ ads per month at a few million in spend that were not profitable and attributes that to a strategy gap, not a volume one.
caveats: Volume without strategy and offer/persona/angle quality does not automatically scale a brand.
Treat 100–300/month as a source-stated heuristic for growth-oriented accounts, not a benchmark you must hit.
Launching volume is not the same as driving results — activity can be mistaken for strategy.

cards.title: Second Ad Account as Risk Hedge and Bid-Logic Diversifier
cards.summary: A secondary ad account on the same pixel with different bid logic can both de-risk a Meta-dependent business and win additional auctions.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to open a second ad account when a store is heavily reliant on one platform for new customer acquisition.
steps: Run the same pixel with different bid logic in a second ad account — e.g. maximize conversions in the main account vs maximize conversion value, cost caps or bid caps in the second — so you enter auctions the primary account isn't bidding on. Point it at the same page or a different page.

Primary purpose: risk. If the main ad account gets banned or billing fails, crank up the second account instead of losing all new customer acquisition for potentially a week. The second account can hold as little as 10% of main spend and still serve as the fallback.
Secondary purpose: incremental volume from effectively the same creative, pixel and page, because a different account bids into different auctions.
The source explicitly warns that the exact tactics here change every ~6 months and gives no fixed tactical prescription; treat this as a strategy to evaluate, not a stable configuration.
Verify current Meta ad account and bid-strategy behaviour in the platform before implementing, and confirm whether your second-account approach fits current policy.
caveats: Could increase CPMs/ad costs through self-competition (cross-bidding). The source notes it's an argued downside that nobody has proven, and that same page + same pixel should limit cross-bidding.
Source advice on this strategy is unstable over time; do not treat it as current universal instruction.

cards.title: International Expansion Without Ad-Account Sprawl
cards.summary: Keep country targeting inside one ad account and only split accounts when you have a real reason such as local-currency billing.
cards.use_when: Planning to sell into new regions and deciding whether each region needs its own ad account or just separate targeting and reporting rules.
steps: The source advises against segmenting countries at ad-account level by default; separate accounts multiply management labour and complexity — the source cites clients running seven accounts for seven regions.
Do country-level work inside one account where possible: use filter rules on country segmentation or on campaign naming to get regional reporting instead of separate accounts.
The one convincing reason the source gives for separate accounts is local-currency billing (e.g. USD account for a US presence, GBP for a UK presence) driven by where your money and bank sit.
When you do expand internationally, still think through the operational complexity: how pages are handled, and how the backend (e.g. Shopify or your hosting region setup) handles each region.
Verify current Meta and payments capabilities for multi-currency before designing the split.
caveats: This is the source's agency-perspective recommendation; a business with in-house teams may weight labour cost differently.
Local-currency billing rationale assumes your banking and accounting structure follows the same logic.

cards.title: Five-Campaign Account Structure for ~$750K/Month Spend
cards.summary: A worked example of a high-spend account: testing, scaling, promo, advertorial and DPA campaigns each with a distinct job.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the campaign-level architecture of a store spending in the high six to seven figures monthly.
steps: Testing campaign: all tests run at ad-set level. The source has seen testing run even at $300K/day budgets and disputes the idea that large accounts should stop testing. ABO or CBO both work at this level — ABO forces spend through new tests, CBO lets the algorithm decide.

Scaling campaign: CBO with one ad set using cost caps. Every 1–2 weeks, take top-performing post IDs from testing and launch them into the scaling campaign. Do not turn them off in testing; keep scaling at ad-set level in the testing campaign too (those ad sets can run into thousands per day). The scaling campaign is a way to squeeze more from an already-proven post.

Promo campaign: separate because promos turn over frequently and would disrupt learning if launched into testing/scaling, and because promos target a different, more price-sensitive customer that should optimise separately. In the example, promos run every 3–4 weeks.
Advertorial campaign: pull advertorials out as a dedicated campaign once they consume a large share of spend (in the example, ~30% of total spend) so the funnel can be KPI'd on its own.

DPA campaign: primarily retargeting existing customers plus some website visitors, run on incremental attribution, kept at relatively low spend in line with frequency. This is an example account, not a template guarantee — adapt to your business's complexities.
caveats: The source states explicitly this will not guarantee results for your business; it is one real account spending ~$750K/month.
The source deliberately does not give a single prescribed structure across the whole $250K–$20M/month range because complexity varies too much.

cards.title: What Stays Fixed as Spend Scales
cards.summary: Four fundamentals — data integrity, commercial alignment, the concept framework, and ad-set/campaign KPI-ing — should never be traded away when adding account layers.
cards.use_when: Auditing a complex high-spend account or deciding whether a new structural element is worth adding.
steps: Data integrity is non-negotiable: every added bit of complexity must still produce readable data you can use to make decisions. If you can't read it, remove the layer.
Commercial alignment is non-negotiable: check the new structure aligns with products, margin, portfolio and personas — don't add complexity for its own sake.
The breakdown effect still applies: ad-level and breakdown-level analysis is no more productive at high spend than at low spend; the principle doesn't change.
The concept framework for launching and testing creative still applies, and the source explicitly recommends it even at $300K/day spend; large accounts typically structure and test creative this way.
Keep KPI-ing at ad-set and campaign level regardless of tier.

Use these as the four gating questions for any restructure: does the structure produce readable data; does it match how the business actually makes money; is it appropriate for the spend tier and creative throughput; are the support layers (DPA, retargeting, website visitors, existing customers) aligned with actual retention.
caveats: If the answer to any of the four questions is no, the source says the account structure is wrong and needs restructuring.
These principles constrain structure but do not prescribe one — the right structure remains business-specific.

cards.title: ABO vs CBO: Choose Your Risk/Efficiency Profile
cards.summary: ABO vs CBO is a risk-vs-efficiency trade-off, not a right answer, and seasonal rotation between them is a legitimate tactic.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to distribute spend across new creative tests, especially in peak vs testing seasons.
steps: CBO = higher efficiency, higher risk. It concentrates spend on the highest-performing ads and ad sets, producing the best blended ROAS, but new ads may get no spend at all — a problem if you just spent heavily on a shoot or an expensive influencer partnership.
ABO = forced spend through every new creative, i.e. you explicitly buy testing coverage regardless of algorithmic preference for efficiency.

If you want partial control within CBO, use minimum and maximum spend limits. The source's preferred structure at high spend: tightly control ~60% of budget with min/max caps and let ~40% flow where Meta wants. The source calls this the best structure they run — but it demands real management oversight and is overkill at low spend (e.g. $10K/month — just run ABO or CBO).

Seasonal rotation: run the higher-risk/higher-efficiency configuration (CBO) in peak periods like Black Friday and Nov–Dec when you just want maximum efficiency and spend; rotate back to ABO in Q1 for a heavy testing environment that isn't artificially inflated by peak conversion rates.
Decide based on your trust in the algorithm: whether you want spend forced through every new creative or whether you accept that Meta only gives spend to ads it predicts will do well.
Regardless of ABO or CBO, keep at least 3 ads per ad set so the ad set can sequence across ads — one ad cannot sequence, and buyers generally need multiple exposures before purchase.
caveats: The source states there is no right or wrong answer; both perform well and the choice is largely preference and historical observation within the account.

One stated exception: with very high AOV and low conversion volume, the source advises against CBO, because CBO prioritises softer high-intent metrics like CTR and CPC and will distribute spend to the best soft-metric ads rather than the ads that drive conversions.
Min/max spend cap management is described as annoying and management-heavy — it only pays off at large spend.

cards.title: Ad Set Composition: 3 to 15 Ads, Same Audience
cards.summary: Keep a minimum of three ads per ad set so they can sequence, and keep every ad in the ad set resonating with the same audience.
cards.use_when: Building ad sets and deciding how many creative assets to place in each one.
steps: Minimum 3 ads per ad set so the ad set can sequence across ads; with one ad there is nothing to sequence across and it just serves repeatedly.

Maximum is effectively open at high spend — the source cites accounts running around 200 creatives in an ad set. For most accounts you don't have the creative volume to support that, and those 200 assets likely span different concepts you shouldn't consolidate.
Working rule of thumb: 3–15 ads per ad set.
All ads in an ad set should resonate with the same audience. This does not mean all ads must be the same stage of awareness — see the separate card on mixing funnel stages inside one ad set.
If you would need to spread concepts across 200 ads, instead add ad-set-level segmentation so each ad set holds a coherent concept.
caveats: The 200-creative example is a practitioner observation, not a recommended target for most stores.
3–15 is described as a rule of thumb, not a hard limit.

cards.title: Consolidate Funnel Stages in One Ad Set to Avoid Biased Readouts
cards.summary: Consolidating top-, mid- and bottom-of-funnel ads in a single ad set makes the concept easier to read than splitting them by awareness stage.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to split a persona's ads by stage of awareness at the ad-set level, or keep them grouped.
steps: Two viable options exist: split awareness stages into separate ad sets, or consolidate top/middle/bottom-of-funnel ads into one ad set. The source leans toward consolidation.

The main argument for consolidation is human bias, not machine learning. If you split, the bottom-of-funnel ad set will show a much higher ROAS (e.g. 6x) than the top-of-funnel ad set (e.g. 2x) because it takes last-click credit for traffic the top-of-funnel ad generated.

The correct action in the split scenario is still to blend the numbers — treat the two ad sets as working together to drive the conversion and scale the concept as a whole. But in practice, and especially with clients, people resist putting more spend into a 2x ad set, so the human decision-making process breaks down.
Consolidating keeps the concept's number as one readable figure (e.g. 4x), which triggers the correct decision: scale it and make more like it.
Keep all ads in the ad set resonating with the same audience; the consolidation is about funnel stage, not about mixing unrelated personas.
Verify current Meta creative-sequence and delivery behaviour in the platform, as this reflects the source's operating experience.
caveats: Option one (splitting) has been seen to work; this is a recommendation with a stated reason (human bias in reading multi-ad-set concepts), not an absolute rule.
Assumes last-click-style attribution skew; check how your attribution model distributes credit before drawing conclusions from a split structure.

cards.title: Name Ad Sets by Persona, Angle, Offer, Content Type, Date
cards.summary: Structured ad-set naming is what makes it possible to filter, bundle and KPI concepts across a campaign after the fact.
cards.use_when: Setting up ad sets or cleaning up an inherited account where you need concept-level reporting.
steps: Avoid batch-style names like 'March 7 creatives' — they carry no concept information and imply you batched multiple concepts together rather than structuring a test.
Name ad sets with the exact persona, angle, offer, then content type (if grouping a content type), then date of launch.
This enables filtering and bundling across a campaign so you can KPI different concepts and read directional creative feedback.
When taking over an account with poor naming, retro-rename historical ad sets to recover some kind of structured historical data, so you can infer what to double down on going forward.
Keep the convention consistent when launching new tests, otherwise the historical read degrades again.
caveats: Retro-renaming recovers structure but cannot recreate data that was never separated at launch.
Exact date/version conventions are your choice — the source's point is that all dimensions must be present in the name.

cards.title: Retargeting Is a Capped Support Layer, Not a Growth Driver
cards.summary: Treat retargeting with a scarcity mindset — minimise spend, consolidate audiences, and manage by frequency and profitability rather than percentage of budget.
cards.use_when: Auditing retargeting and existing-customer spend allocation in an ad account.
steps: Pull audience-segment breakdowns and check total spend distribution. The source describes audits where ~50% of spend goes to existing customers and engaged audiences — support spend that is not driving incremental new customer growth and is often not even incremental.
Cold/new customer acquisition = abundance mindset: constantly ask where you can spend more, as long as the exchange is profitable (e.g. $1 in returns $4 out) — keep pushing money there.
Existing customer/retargeting = scarcity mindset: constantly ask where you can take money out. Look across Meta, TikTok, Pinterest and pull budget from wherever you're overspending.

Consolidate retargeting audiences. Hyper-segmentation by landing page visited, add-to-cart vs initiate-checkout vs website visitors, etc., only increases CPMs; the source states the CPM increase is never outweighed by the conversion rate increase.

Make frequency the core KPI on retargeting campaigns alongside incremental revenue: how many times per week/month are you retargeting existing and engaged audiences, and is that subjectively too high or too low? (The source's example of 30 retargets a month is framed as intuitively too high.)
Verify current platform audience-consolidation and reporting behaviour before restructuring.
caveats: The 50% existing-customer spend figure is an example the source has seen repeatedly in audits, not a threshold.
Frequency tolerance is subjective and business-specific; the source presents it as a judgement call, not a benchmark.

cards.title: DPAs Only Look Great Because They Sit at the Point of Purchase
cards.summary: DPA ROAS is inflated by last-click position, and DPA performance is a direct reflection of top-of-funnel investment — starving the top causes a DPA death spiral.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much to spend on dynamic product ads and whether to cut creative/top-of-funnel budget because DPA ROAS looks strong.
steps: Accept that DPAs place right before the moment of purchase and therefore take more credit than they should; their ROAS looks far better than the true incremental contribution.
Assess DPA return on ad spend using 7-day click or incremental attribution rather than a default/last-click read.
Treat DPA performance as a direct reflection of top-of-funnel investment: increase top-of-funnel budget and DPA ROAS rises; decrease top-of-funnel and DPA performance falls.

The 'DPA death spiral' pattern: brands seeing strong-looking DPA figures keep increasing DPA budget (in the source's audit examples, up to ~80% of spend) while reducing creative production and top-of-funnel allocation; the account then declines over subsequent months and it becomes too late to fix.
Keep DPAs in a dedicated, relatively low-spend campaign run on incremental attribution and managed in line with frequency, as in the source's worked account example.
DPAs are described as especially relevant for fashion and for large catalogues/SKU counts.
caveats: The death-spiral accounts are examples the source audited (fashion brands), not a general law with measured effect sizes.
DYPA personalisation depends on the pixel firing correct data — if it doesn't, retargeting relevance suffers.
Attribution model specifics should be verified in the current platform interface.

cards.title: Budget Existing-Customer Spend in Dollars, Not as a Percentage
cards.summary: Percentage-of-spend targets for existing customers are the wrong frame; decide by profitability and by a dollar budget derived from customers × CPM × desired frequency.
cards.use_when: Setting existing-customer and retargeting budget for a period, or reviewing whether a spend-cap percentage is meaningful.
steps: Ignore the 'what % should go to existing customers' frame (the source traces this mindset to Meta's advantage+ existing customer spend cap input) because the percentage shifts with pool size and with how much budget you're putting to new customer acquisition, making it useless as a metric.
Assess two questions instead. First, is it profitable: if you spent another $10 or $1,000 a day on existing customers, would the returned revenue pay for the spend and leave profit?

Second, what is frequency? It's a softer but more real-time signal. A 20% allocation with a frequency of 50 per 30 days is a problem; a 20% allocation with frequency of 1 is probably substantial underspending.
Set the budget as a dollar figure: number of customers × CPM × desired frequency per month = monthly budget toward that existing-customer audience.
Re-derive this figure as the customer pool and CPMs change, rather than tracking the percentage.
caveats: The CPM × customers × frequency formula is a stated calculation method; validate that your available CPM figures reflect the audiences you're actually targeting.
Frequency targets remain a judgement call — the source frames these as sanity checks, not thresholds.

cards.title: Settings to Turn Off: Flexible Ads, One-Day View, Auto Creative Optimisations
cards.summary: Disable settings that destroy readout clarity or shift budget attribution — flexible ads, one-day view attribution in decisions, and Advantage+ creative auto-optimisations at both ad and advertiser level.
cards.use_when: Setting up or cleaning a store's ad account settings and creative configuration.
steps: Turn off flexible ads. They package multiple creatives into one ad, so if the ad performs you don't know which creative drove it — the readout fails the data-integrity test. If used only to work around the page limit, load very similar creative so a winner at least tells you 'this type of ad' works.

Turn off one-day view attribution, or at minimum exclude it from budget-allocation decisions at ad-set level, because the source says it substantially overattributes based on existing customer revenue.

Check all Advantage+ creative optimisations: in advertiser settings, go to the creative sub-dropdown where automated rules are enabled that will effectively flip your creative optimisation settings back on over time. Turn these off at the advertiser setting level, not just per ad.
Verify current Meta settings paths and option names in the ad manager before acting — interface naming changes.

Additional flexible-ads drawbacks stated by the source: you lose control over image cropping (1:1 served in stories, stories randomly cropped into feed), and Meta may string flexible creatives into a carousel you did not approve.
caveats: These are the source agency's preferences grounded in data-readability and creative control; other accounts have reportedly made flexible ads work, so treat as a deliberate trade-off rather than a platform rule.
Attribution settings and Advantage+ defaults change; always confirm in the current interface.

cards.title: Maintain Audience Segment Sync Audit (CRM → Meta)
cards.summary: Periodically verify that the CRM-to-Meta audience segment sync hasn't broken, otherwise existing customers get treated as new and spend integrity erodes.
cards.use_when: During routine account audits; especially after third-party tooling or CRM changes.
steps: At regular cadence, check that audience segments syncing from CRM tooling (the source names Klaviyo to Meta) are still flowing correctly.
The source observes these syncs break periodically; when they break, existing customers stop being excluded or correctly classified, so you spend on existing customers thinking they're new.
Consequence: forecast growth integrity erodes and budget flows to places you don't want; incremental new-customer reporting becomes unreliable.
When a break is found, fix the sync and re-check recent spend against existing-customer reporting for the affected period.
Confirm current integration and segment-sync behaviour in your tooling before relying on it.
caveats: The Klaviyo-to-Meta example is the source's observed case; other connector pairs may have different failure modes.
This is an audit practice — not a one-time setup step.

cards.title: Calculate Test Budget from Conversions, CPA and Duration
cards.summary: Set test budgets by defining the statistical threshold and the learning window first, then dividing threshold × expected CPA by days.
cards.use_when: Planning a creative or concept test and sizing the daily budget so it reaches a conclusion in the timeframe you chose.
steps: Answer two questions before building the test: what is the statistical threshold in conversions (5, 10, 20 — you decide), and how quickly do you want to learn (3, 7, 30 days)?
Compute the daily test budget: (target conversions × expected CPA) ÷ test duration in days.
Worked example: 20 target conversions at $100 CPA over 14 days = $143/day.

Compare against Meta's standard advice of 50 conversions per 7 days for exiting the learning phase: back-propagating that at the same $100 CPA over 7 days gives $714/day for a single concept ad-set test, which becomes $7,000/day if you want 5–10 tests running. The source describes this as unrealistic for 99% of advertisers.
The consequence is to set your own threshold and window rather than defaulting to the platform's learning-phase guidance, and to budget each testing ad set accordingly.
Define in advance what result moves the test out of testing (winner to scale) and what kills it.
caveats: The threshold and duration are your choices; the source gives 5/10/20 as example thresholds rather than established constants.
$100 CPA and 20/14-day figures are illustrative worked examples.
Statistical significance in-platform is not the same as statistically rigorous inference; treat thresholds as operational aids.

cards.title: Creative as the Growth Lever, Portfolio Model Over Hero Ads
cards.summary: Meta has compressed media-buying arbitrage and left creative as the leverage point; diversify spend across many ads rather than betting on a few winners that will fatigue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of the store's investment goes into creative production vs media-buying tactics, and how to manage creative risk.
steps: Accept the source's framing: targeting is fully automated (broad targeting recommended for ~99% of advertisers), Andromeda optimises creative distribution, and platforms favour consolidation — so classic media-buying hacks (duplicating ad sets, bespoke bidding tricks) no longer produce large arbitrage.

Choose the diversified portfolio: e.g. three ads holding $1,000/day at a blended 4x vs one ad holding all of it at 4x. Prefer the diversified structure because a single creative fatiguing ends the account, while in the three-ad structure the others pick up the slack.
Treat creative as a revenue driver, not a cost centre. The creative drives revenue; the platform only distributes it, and the same creative can earn organic distribution.
Mitigate the risk the source describes in businesses that built eight-figure revenue on three creatives that then fatigued together — recoveries are hard at that point.

Apply the thesis practically: invest in creative strategy, briefing and production capacity so that more ads hold more spend, and analyse creative in the account to create a flywheel. Media buying is described as not being the advantage right now.
caveats: This is the source's strong, explicit opinion for 2026–2027: 'media buying fundamentally is not your advantage right now' — it's a strategic stance, not a platform fact.
The eight-figure, three-creative case is a narrated example, not a measured result.

cards.title: Diagnose Creative Bottlenecks Before Adding Volume
cards.summary: Name which creative bottleneck is actually constraining growth — quality, format diversity, funnel-stage coverage, partnership ads, or strategy — before spending more on volume.
cards.use_when: When creative output is high but growth is flat or unprofitable, or before deciding what to change in the creative system.
steps: List the candidate bottlenecks: quality of creative; format diversification; quantity sitting at each awareness stage (e.g. nowhere near enough top-of-funnel assets to support the scale you want); absence of partnership ads or other distribution-unlocking approaches.

Identify which one is actually limiting the account before adding activity, because most people don't understand all the bottlenecks that exist and therefore misdiagnose, then focus on activity that doesn't move the needle.

Example the source cites: accounts launching 2,000+ ads a month at a few million in spend that were not profitable — they thought volume would unlock growth and were fixing something that didn't need fixing.

Also avoid conflating activity with strategy: doubling ad volume is not a growth plan by itself (the source's answer to 'do I just launch 40 more ads?' is that if it were that simple everyone would do it).
When quality, offer, persona and angle are right, the source says you shouldn't need anywhere near 2,000 ads a month to hit that spend level.
Once the true bottleneck is named, direct the fix there (e.g. more top-of-funnel assets, new formats, partnership ads) rather than to raw volume.
caveats: The 2,000-ad, few-million-spend example is the source's observation of two accounts, not a benchmark.
There is no diagnostic checklist provided beyond the bottleneck categories — naming yours requires reviewing your own account data.

cards.title: How Andromeda Reversed Targeting: Ads Go In, Meta Finds the Audience
cards.summary: In the source's simplification, pre-Andromeda you chose an interest then loaded creative; post-Andromeda you load creative with no targeting and Meta infers the audience from the ads themselves.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much effort to put into interest/audience targeting versus into the content of the creative itself.
steps: Prioritise creative content that Meta can interpret: transcript, words in the ad, copy, and historical conversion data are what the source says Meta reads to place your ads.
Pre-Andromeda (as the source simplifies it) you selected an interest and loaded creatives under it — ads were matched to a chosen audience.
Post-Andromeda the direction is reversed: put the ads in without selecting targeting, and Meta finds people who match the creative based on its understanding of the ad content and conversion history.
Practical consequence for the store: clarity of persona, angle and offer in the ad itself becomes the targeting. Ambiguous creative gives the algorithm less to work with.

Pair this with the source's recommendation of broad targeting for ~99% of advertisers, and keep concept structure to understand which creative/audience combinations are actually working since you can't set audiences by hand.
Verify how current Meta delivery and targeting options behave before switching off your targeting entirely.
caveats: The source explicitly presents the pre/post-Andromeda contrast as a simplification for teaching, and as their own operational understanding, not a documented Meta specification.
Mechanism details (using repurposed training GPUs per the source) are context, not a guarantee of current system behaviour.
